full_judgment: 14. This Court on a consideration of the above is satisfied that the Letters of Guarantee as issued in the two Suits are governed by specific legislative and common law standards as well as rules internal to the P&I club's operations that create a regime of an assumption of immediate liability by a guarantor thereunder that ranges from being coextensive to those of the principal debtor to that of being capable of enforcement individually and exclusively of the liability of the principal debtor. It is equally clear that the essential character of such Letters of Guarantee being however, qualified by the fact that these while establishing privity of contract between the guarantor and the creditor do not at the same time permit of undertakings before the Court per se, thereby, consequentially requiring judicial pronouncements for due execution of the same. This can only be achieved upon the guarantor, and by extension the Letters of Guarantee, being brought specifically within the purview of the jurisdiction of this Court. By that reason this Court is satisfied that the P&I clubs in both the suits have properly been impleaded as defendant No. 1 in each Suit and by necessity leading to their correspondents in Bangladesh being impleaded as parties as well. That being the case, this Court finds no hindrance to accepting the view that the said defendants are indeed, necessary and proper parties as contemplated under the various provisions of the Code. This is because some relief consequent to the Letters of Guarantee is seen by this Court to lie against the said defendants and the Suits cannot, therefore, be completely decided and no effective decree consequentially made in their absence.
